C8 — when a bone's reaction is along its axis. Probes: the two-force-member assumption behind R = |λ|L, and recognizing when a mid-shaft load makes it bend instead (§7, §8).

In the lab of §7 each joint reaction came out along its bone, $R=|\lambda|L$. What assumption forces the reaction to be axial, and what real feature of a limb breaks it?

Show solution

Each bone in §7 is massless and touched only at its two endpoints — the joints. A rigid body loaded at only two points is a two-force member: equilibrium forces those two forces to be equal, opposite, and directed along the line joining them, i.e. along the bone. That is why the reaction magnitude is $R=|\lambda|L$ and its line of action is the bone axis. The assumption breaks the moment a force acts between the ends — a muscle inserting mid-shaft, or the bone's own distributed weight. Then the bone carries a transverse load and bends, and we need the beam mechanics of Module 2 rather than a single axial number.

C9 — force is not the whole story: pressure. Probes: that pressure depends on contact area as well as force — why joint congruence matters (§5).

Two joints transmit the same reaction force, but one spreads it over twice the contact area. Using the mean-pressure idea of §5, which cartilage is at greater risk, and why does joint congruence matter as much as load?

Show solution

Mean contact pressure is $p=F/A$ (§5): for a fixed force, doubling the contact area halves the pressure. The cartilage on the smaller contact sees the higher pressure and is at greater risk. Congruence matters because it sets $A$: well-matched (congruent) surfaces share the load over a broad patch and keep the peak pressure low, while an incongruent (cam-shaped) joint concentrates the same force on a small patch, spiking the local pressure toward cartilage damage and osteoarthritis. Survival is governed by force and the area it is spread over — not force alone.

C10 — more muscles than freedoms. Probes: muscle redundancy — that motion alone under-determines muscle forces and the joint reaction, so co-contraction matters (§8).

A single joint is spanned by several muscles, but it has only one (or a few) degrees of freedom. Does knowing the joint's motion determine each muscle's force? What does that imply for the joint reaction, and how is the ambiguity resolved?

Show solution

No. The joint's motion fixes only the net torque the muscles must produce; with more muscles than degrees of freedom, infinitely many force combinations give that same torque. So the individual muscle forces — and therefore the joint reaction they press across the surfaces — are not determined by kinematics alone. In particular, agonist–antagonist co-contraction (both pulling at once) adds no net torque but raises the joint reaction sharply. Resolving the split needs an extra principle — an optimization criterion such as minimal effort or fatigue — the muscle-redundancy problem flagged in §8 and taken up in later modules.

9.3 Derivational problems

Ten problems to derive — each rebuilds or extends a result from the module. Work the algebra before opening the solution. Two of the ten close with a numerical check: D1 recovers $|\lambda|L=mg$ for a hanging mass, and D3 reproduces the $2.5\,W$ of (4.1).

D1 — the static multiplier, and a sanity check. Probes: specializing the general multiplier formula to statics, and validating it against a known limit (§3, §7.2).

Starting from the multiplier formula of §3, $$\lambda = -\bigl(J_c M^{-1} J_c^{\mathsf T}\bigr)^{-1}\bigl(J_c M^{-1}(Q-c)+\dot J_c\,\dot q\bigr),$$ specialise it to an instant of rest ($\dot q=0$) in Cartesian coordinates (where $c=0$ and gravity sits in $Q$). Then apply the result to a single mass $m$ on a rigid rod of length $L$, hanging straight down, and show the pivot reaction equals the weight.

Show solution

With $\dot q=0$, the term $\dot J_c\dot q$ vanishes, and with $c=0$ the formula collapses to

$$\boxed{\;\lambda = -\bigl(J_c M^{-1} J_c^{\mathsf T}\bigr)^{-1} J_c M^{-1} Q.\;}$$

For the pendulum, take $q=(x,y)$ with $y$ up, $M=mI_2$, gravity $Q=(0,-mg)$, and the rod constraint $g=\tfrac12(x^2+y^2-L^2)$, so $J_c=(x,\,y)$. Then $M^{-1}=\tfrac1m I_2$ and

$$J_c M^{-1} J_c^{\mathsf T}=\frac{x^2+y^2}{m}=\frac{L^2}{m},\qquad J_c M^{-1} Q=\frac{1}{m}(x\cdot 0 + y\cdot(-mg))=-yg.$$

Hanging straight down means $x=0,\ y=-L$, so $J_c M^{-1}Q=Lg$ and

$$\lambda=-\frac{m}{L^2}\,(Lg)=-\frac{mg}{L}\quad\Rightarrow\quad |\lambda|\,L = mg.$$

The joint-reaction rule $R=|\lambda|L$ of §7.2 then gives a pivot reaction of exactly $mg$ — the pivot carries the full weight, as it must. (Numerically, $m=1\ \mathrm{kg},\,L=0.3\ \mathrm m$ gives $|\lambda|L=9.81\ \mathrm N=mg$ to machine precision.)

D2 — the elbow joint reaction. Probes: building a joint reaction from a free-body diagram, and seeing why it dwarfs the load it holds (§4, Module 1).

A forearm holds a weight $W_{\text{load}}$ at a distance $L$ from the elbow. The biceps inserts a short distance $d\ (\ll L)$ from the joint, and the forearm-plus-hand weight $W_f$ acts at its center of mass a distance $c$ from the joint. Taking moments about the elbow, find the muscle force $F_m$ and the joint reaction $R$, then evaluate for the reference human of Module 1: $W_{\text{load}}=49\ \mathrm N$ (a 5 kg bag), $L=0.35\ \mathrm m$, $d=0.03\ \mathrm m$, $W_f=15\ \mathrm N$, $c=0.116\ \mathrm m$. Then repeat with $d=0.05\ \mathrm m$ and say, in one sentence, what a 2 cm change in insertion buys the joint.

Show solution

Moment balance about the elbow (the joint reaction passes through the joint and so contributes no moment about it):

$$F_m\,d = W_{\text{load}}\,L + W_f\,c\ \Rightarrow\ F_m=\frac{W_{\text{load}}L+W_f c}{d}.$$

Vertical force balance gives the joint reaction $R=F_m-W_{\text{load}}-W_f$. With the reference-human values, $F_m=\dfrac{49(0.35)+15(0.116)}{0.03}=630\ \mathrm N$ and $R=630-49-15=566\ \mathrm N$: about $11.6\times$ the weight being held, and $0.82$ times the body weight of a 70 kg adult. These are exactly the numbers of §4.1. Moving the insertion out to $d=0.05\ \mathrm m$ gives $F_m=378\ \mathrm N$ and $R=314\ \mathrm N$: a 67 % longer lever cuts both the muscle force and the joint load by 40 %, which is why the moment arm, not the load, is the quantity worth knowing. The short insertion lever forces a large muscle force, and the joint must carry almost all of it: the amplification of §4.

D3 — the hip in single-leg stance. Probes: the abductor-lever model behind the few-times-body-weight hip reaction (§4.2).

In single-leg stance the hip abductors, on a lever $a$ from the joint, balance the supported weight $W_s$ (body weight $W$ less the stance leg, $W_s=\tfrac56 W$, the value of §4.2) acting at a lever $b$. Find the abductor force and show the hip reaction $R$ is a few times body weight when $b/a\approx 2$.

Show solution

Moments about the femoral head: $F_{ab}\,a = W_s\,b$, so $F_{ab}=W_s\,(b/a)$. Treating the abductor pull and the supported weight as vertical and co-linear (the tilted-muscle correction of §4.2 raises the magnitude to $2.7\,W$), vertical balance gives $R = W_s\bigl(1+b/a\bigr)$. With $b/a\approx2$ and $W_s=\tfrac56 W$, $R = \tfrac56(3)\,W = 2.5\,W$: equation (4.1) of §4.2, rederived. It sits just below the $\approx2.3$–$2.9\,W$ that in-vivo telemetry reads in slow level walking (§8), which is the right comparison, because this is a static estimate and telemetry measures a moving joint.

D4 — differentiate the constraint twice. Probes: turning a position constraint into the acceleration-level equation that closes the KKT system (§3.3).

Starting from a holonomic constraint $g(q)=0$, differentiate twice in time to obtain the velocity- and acceleration-level constraints. Identify the constraint Jacobian $J_c$ and the term $\dot J_c\dot q$.

Show solution

Differentiate once by the chain rule:

$$\frac{d}{dt}g(q)=\frac{\partial g}{\partial q}\dot q = J_c\,\dot q = 0,$$

so the velocity stays tangent to the surface. Differentiate again:

$$\frac{d}{dt}\bigl(J_c\dot q\bigr)=J_c\,\ddot q+\dot J_c\,\dot q = 0.$$

These $m$ acceleration equations are the rows that join the $n$ dynamical equations $M\ddot q+c=Q+J_c^{\mathsf T}\lambda$ to close the KKT system (3.4). The $\dot J_c\dot q$ term is the centripetal part: not a force, but the acceleration that $J_c\ddot q$ must cancel merely to keep the motion curving along the constraint.

D5 — the multiplier by elimination. Probes: solving the saddle-point KKT system for $\lambda$ — the Schur-complement step behind Proposition 3.2 (§3.3).

From the block (KKT) system, eliminate the acceleration $\ddot q$ to derive the closed form $\lambda=-\bigl(J_cM^{-1}J_c^{\mathsf T}\bigr)^{-1}\bigl(J_cM^{-1}(Q-c)+\dot J_c\dot q\bigr).$

Show solution

The top block is $M\ddot q + c = Q + J_c^{\mathsf T}\lambda$, so

$$\ddot q = M^{-1}\bigl(Q-c+J_c^{\mathsf T}\lambda\bigr).$$

Substitute into the acceleration constraint $J_c\ddot q=-\dot J_c\dot q$:

$$J_cM^{-1}\bigl(Q-c+J_c^{\mathsf T}\lambda\bigr)=-\dot J_c\dot q\ \Rightarrow\ \bigl(J_cM^{-1}J_c^{\mathsf T}\bigr)\lambda=-\dot J_c\dot q-J_cM^{-1}(Q-c),$$

which inverts to Proposition 3.2. The matrix $J_cM^{-1}J_c^{\mathsf T}$ (the constraint's effective inverse inertia) is invertible whenever $J_c$ has full row rank — i.e. the constraints are independent.

D6 — the mobility of a closed chain. Probes: the planar mobility (Grübler) count, and why closing a loop spends degrees of freedom (§1, §2).

For a planar mechanism of $n$ rigid links (counting the fixed ground as one) joined by $j$ pin joints, derive the mobility formula and apply it to (a) an open three-link arm pinned to ground, and (b) two rigid legs joining a pelvis to the ground.

Show solution

Each free planar link has $3$ freedoms; the $n-1$ moving links give $3(n-1)$. Each pin joint allows only a relative rotation, removing $2$:

$$\boxed{\ \text{DOF}=3(n-1)-2j.\ }$$

(a) Open arm: $n=4$ (three links + ground), $j=3$ pins, DOF $=3(3)-2(3)=3$ — the three joint angles. (b) Two-leg stance: $n=4$ (pelvis + two legs + ground), $j=4$ pins, DOF $=3(3)-2(4)=1$. The extra pin from closing the loop drops the count from $3$ to $1$: a closed chain trades mobility for rigidity, the opposite of the open limbs of §2.

D7 — from joint force to contact pressure. Probes: converting a joint reaction into a peak cartilage pressure, and the Hertz exponents (§5).

(a) Write the mean pressure for a force $F$ spread over area $A$. (b) For a sphere of radius $R$ pressed on a flat elastic surface of effective modulus $E^*$, the contact radius obeys $a\propto\bigl(FR/E^*\bigr)^{1/3}$ and the peak pressure is $p_0=3F/(2\pi a^2)$. Derive how $p_0$ scales with $F$, $E^*$ and $R$.

Show solution

(a) $p_{\text{mean}}=F/A$. (b) With $a^2\propto(FR/E^*)^{2/3}$,

$$p_0=\frac{3F}{2\pi a^2}\ \propto\ \frac{F}{(FR/E^*)^{2/3}}=F^{1/3}\,E^{*\,2/3}\,R^{-2/3}.$$

Peak pressure rises only as the cube root of force but as the two-thirds power of stiffness, and falls with radius. So a stiffer or sharper (small-$R$, incongruent) contact is punishing even at modest load — the reason cartilage is soft and joints are congruent (§5; Module 4).

D8 — the stability ratio. Probes: deriving $S=\tan\beta$ from the rim-climb force balance (§6).

A head is pressed into its socket by a compressive force $N$ along the socket axis and pushed sideways by a destabilizing force $F_t$. It dislocates by climbing over the socket rim, which sits at angle $\beta$ from the axis. Show the head escapes when $F_t=N\tan\beta$, i.e. the stability ratio is $S=\tan\beta$.

Show solution

At the point of escape the head is on the verge of riding up the rim. Resolve forces along the rim surface, whose normal makes angle $\beta$ with the socket axis. The compressive force $N$ supplies a restoring component $N\sin\beta$ along the rim, opposed by the driving component $F_t\cos\beta$. Setting them equal at the threshold,

$$F_t\cos\beta = N\sin\beta\ \Rightarrow\ \boxed{\,F_t=N\tan\beta,\quad S\equiv\frac{F_t}{N}=\tan\beta.\,}$$

A deeper socket (larger $\beta$) needs a larger sideways force to dislocate — the hip-versus-shoulder contrast of §6.

D9 — the two-link mass matrix. Probes: assembling $M(q)$ in joint-angle coordinates and seeing its configuration dependence — the contrast with the constant Cartesian $M$ of §7.2.

For a planar two-link limb with joint angles $(\theta_1,\theta_2)$, where $\theta_1$ is measured from the horizontal and $\theta_2$ is the relative angle at the elbow (so the second link points along $\theta_1+\theta_2$), point masses $m_1,m_2$ at the link ends, and lengths $L_1,L_2$, derive the mass matrix from the kinetic energy and show that $M_{11}$ depends on $\theta_2$.

Show solution

With $\phi=\theta_1+\theta_2$, the elbow is at $L_1(\cos\theta_1,\sin\theta_1)$ and the hand at that plus $L_2(\cos\phi,\sin\phi)$. Forming $T=\tfrac12 m_1\lVert\dot p_1\rVert^2+\tfrac12 m_2\lVert\dot p_2\rVert^2$ and reading off $T=\tfrac12\dot q^{\mathsf T}M\dot q$ gives

$$M=\begin{bmatrix}(m_1+m_2)L_1^2+m_2L_2^2+2m_2L_1L_2\cos\theta_2 & m_2L_2^2+m_2L_1L_2\cos\theta_2\\[2pt] m_2L_2^2+m_2L_1L_2\cos\theta_2 & m_2L_2^2\end{bmatrix}.$$

Every entry but $M_{22}$ carries a $\cos\theta_2$: the inertia felt at the shoulder changes as the elbow bends. Compare the constant diagonal $M$ that redundant Cartesian coordinates gave in §7.2 — the trade-off of §3.5 made concrete.

D10 — the pendulum tension. Probes: combining energy conservation with the radial Newton equation to recover $T(\theta)$ (§3.4).

A pendulum (mass $m$, length $L$) is released from rest at angle $\theta_0$ and swings to angle $\theta$ from the vertical. Derive the rod tension $T(\theta)=mg\,(3\cos\theta-2\cos\theta_0)$.

Show solution

Energy conservation from the release point ($v=0$ at $\theta_0$) to angle $\theta$ gives

$$\tfrac12 m v^2 = mgL(\cos\theta-\cos\theta_0)\ \Rightarrow\ v^2=2gL(\cos\theta-\cos\theta_0).$$

Newton's law along the rod (centripetal, toward the pivot): $T-mg\cos\theta = m v^2/L$, so

$$T=mg\cos\theta+\frac{m v^2}{L}=mg\cos\theta+2mg(\cos\theta-\cos\theta_0)=mg\,(3\cos\theta-2\cos\theta_0).$$

At the bottom ($\theta=0$) the tension peaks at $mg(3-2\cos\theta_0)$; this is the measured rod force whose multiplier was computed in §3.4.

9.4 Computational problems

Ten problems to compute. Each is a small edit to the lab script of §7.4. Wrap that script's setup and loop in one function, save the file as lab.py, and give it exactly this signature, so that every block below can say from lab import run:

def run(L1=0.30, L2=0.30, m1=2.0, m2=1.5, mL=0.0, g=9.81, yh=-0.48,
        amp=40.0, gd=40.0, gp=40.0, dt=5e-5, nstep=40000,
        wall=False, xw=0.30):
    '''Run the section 7.4 lab and return its history dict h.

    h has keys 't', 'Rs', 'Re', 'Nc', 'x2', 'gerr', each a NumPy
    array of length nstep.  Save this file as lab.py.
    '''

Four of those arguments do more than set a number, and the solutions below rely on all four. mL is a mass held at the hand; it enters only through the applied force, as $-(m_2+m_L)g$ in the fourth slot of $Q$, and never through $M$, which stays $\operatorname{diag}(m_1,m_1,m_2,m_2)$. That is a deliberate idealization, named here because problem K1's headline result depends on it: this load carries its weight but not its inertia. amp is the release angle in degrees off the hanging pose, and run builds its own start pose from it — $x_1=L_1\cos\theta$ and $y_1=L_1\sin\theta$ with $\theta=-90^\circ+\texttt{amp}$, then $y_2=y_h$ and $x_2=x_1+\sqrt{L_2^2-(y_h-y_1)^2}$ — so that changing $L_2$, $y_h$ or the amplitude can never leave the limb sitting off its own constraint surface. wall=True swaps the third constraint from $g_3=y_2-y_h$ to $g_3=x_2-x_w$, its Jacobian row from $[0,0,0,1]$ to $[0,0,1,0]$, and the start pose to one with the hand on the wall. gd and gp are the Baumgarte gains $\gamma_d,\gamma_p$ of §7.3; setting both to zero turns stabilization off. Predict each result before you run it. Every number quoted in the solutions below is printed by the code shown with it.

K1 — verify the load path. Probes: quantifying the load-path principle — confirming a vertical load routes entirely to the constraint, not the joints (§7).

Take the runnable code of §7.4. Add a held mass $m_L$ in the hand by changing only the applied-force line, so the hand's downward weight becomes $(m_2+m_L)g$:

mL = 5.0                                   # held hand mass (kg)
# the only change from the lab script of section 7.4
Q = np.array([0, -m1*g, 0, -(m2+mL)*g])

Run it for $m_L=0,\ 5,\ 10\ \mathrm{kg}$. Predict, then check: how does the peak contact force change, and how does the peak shoulder reaction change?

Show solution

The contact force rises by exactly the added weight $m_L g$, while the shoulder and elbow reactions do not move at all:

held mass $m_L$peak contact $\lambda_3$increasepeak shoulder $R_s$
$0\ \mathrm{kg}$$22.3\ \mathrm N$—$32.6\ \mathrm N$
$5\ \mathrm{kg}$$71.4\ \mathrm N$$+49.1\ \mathrm N=5g$$32.6\ \mathrm N$
$10\ \mathrm{kg}$$120.4\ \mathrm N$$+98.1\ \mathrm N=10g$$32.6\ \mathrm N$

This is Problem 1(a) made quantitative, and the cancellation is exact rather than approximate. The held weight adds $-m_Lg$ to the fourth slot of $Q$ and to no other slot, while the rail's constraint gradient is $\nabla g_3=(0,0,0,1)$, which points into that slot and no other. The addition can therefore be written $J_c^{\mathsf T}\delta$ with $\delta=(0,0,-m_Lg)$, and substituting it into (7.6) leaves the acceleration block untouched and moves only the multiplier, $\lambda_3\to\lambda_3+m_Lg$. So the contact absorbs precisely $m_Lg$, the joints never feel it, and the trajectory does not depend on $m_L$ at all — which is why the table's increments are $5g$ and $10g$ exactly, not to two figures.

What that exactness costs. It belongs to the model, not to a real bag. As the preamble to these problems said, $m_L$ enters $Q$ but not $M$: this load has weight and no inertia, and the proof just given used precisely that, because a change in $M$ is not of the form $J_c^{\mathsf T}\delta$. Give the load its inertia as well — M = np.diag([m1, m1, m2 + mL, m2 + mL]) — and the invariance goes. Over the same $m_L=0,\ 5,\ 10\ \mathrm{kg}$ sweep the peak shoulder reaction then runs $32.6\to57.5\to79.7\ \mathrm N$ and the peak contact $22.3\to75.0\to130.9\ \mathrm N$, because the shoulder pin must now accelerate a hand nearly eight times heavier. The swing is in fact slower — the peak speed falls from $1.26$ to $0.66\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}$ and the peak $|\dot J_c\dot q|$ from $0.84$ to $0.43$ — so it is not that the limb swings harder; it is that the inertial part of the reaction scales with the mass being moved, and the extra mass more than repays the lost speed. The load-path lesson survives and sharpens; only the exact cancellation is a property of the inertia-free load, and anyone modelling a real carried bag must add $m_L$ in both places. Going further: swap the rail for a wall (constraint x2 - xw, Jacobian row [0,0,1,0]) and the same held weight drives the shoulder reaction up instead — Problem 1(c), and K2 next.

K2 — swap the rail for a wall. Probes: that the constraint normal sets the load path — a vertical load reaches the joints only when the surface cannot carry it (§7, Problem C1).

Replace the horizontal rail with a frictionless vertical wall that holds the hand at $x=x_w$ (two-sided, like the rail), by changing the third constraint to $g_3=x_2-x_w$ with $x_w=0.30\ \mathrm m$ (Jacobian row $[0,0,1,0]$), and starting the hand on the wall instead of on the rail. Add a held mass $m_L$ at the hand. Predict, then check: does a vertical hand-load now reach the shoulder, and by how much?

import numpy as np
from lab import run          # the section 7.4 script, wrapped as a function

for mL in (0.0, 5.0, 10.0):
    rail = run(mL=mL)
    wall = run(mL=mL, wall=True, xw=0.30)
    print(f"mL={mL:4.1f} | rail Rs {rail['Rs'].max():7.2f}"
          f" contact {rail['Nc'].max():7.2f}"
          f" | wall Rs {wall['Rs'].max():7.2f}")
# -> mL= 0.0 | rail Rs   32.61 contact   22.32 | wall Rs   57.88
# -> mL= 5.0 | rail Rs   32.61 contact   71.37 | wall Rs  121.22
# -> mL=10.0 | rail Rs   32.61 contact  120.42 | wall Rs  187.28
#    (newtons; peak over the swing)
Show solution

The wall's constraint gradient is horizontal, so its reaction is horizontal. A vertical hand-load is now orthogonal to the only direction the contact can supply force in, so the surface takes none of it and the bones must carry all of it to the pin. The contrast is stark. On the rail the peak shoulder reaction is $32.6\ \mathrm N$ whatever the load: the contact swallows the whole of $m_Lg$, rising $22.3\to120.4\ \mathrm N$ as $m_L$ goes $0\to10\ \mathrm{kg}$. (That flat $32.6$ is the inertia-free load of K1 at work; give $m_L$ its inertia too and the rail figure rises to $32.6\to79.7\ \mathrm N$, still far under the wall's.) On the wall the peak shoulder reaction climbs $57.9\to121.2\to187.3\ \mathrm N$ over the same sweep, a factor of $3.2$. (The two runs start from different poses, hand on the rail at $x_2=0.358\ \mathrm m$ and hand on the wall at $x_w=0.30\ \mathrm m$, so compare the trends, not the two zero-load values.) The added $98.1\ \mathrm N$ of weight raises the peak shoulder reaction by $129.4\ \mathrm N$, more than the weight itself, because the heavier hand also swings harder and the $\dot J_c\dot q$ term of §3.3 grows with it. This is problem C1(c) made quantitative, and it is the load-path principle as a design rule: a constraint carries only what is aligned with its normal, and the skeleton carries the rest.

K3 — scale every mass. Probes: that under gravity the motion is mass-independent while forces scale with mass — Galileo, in the joint reaction (§7.6).

Multiply every mass by a factor $k$. Predict, then check, the effect on the joint reactions and on the trajectory.

k = 2.0
m1, m2 = k*2.0, k*1.5            # scale both segment masses
Show solution

Gravity gives every mass the same acceleration, so the trajectory is identical for all $k$ (the hand sweeps the same $0.358\to-0.027\ \mathrm m$), while every force scales exactly by $k$: peak $R_s=16.3,\ 32.6,\ 65.2\ \mathrm N$ for $k=\tfrac12,1,2$. Doubling the limb's mass doubles every joint reaction but changes nothing about how it moves — Galileo's observation, read off the multiplier.

K4 — lengthen the forearm. Probes: separating what sets the reaction (weight and dynamics) from what does not (segment length, here) (§7.6).

Lengthen the forearm $L_2$ (dropping the rail to keep $\approx80\%$ of full reach). How sensitive is the peak shoulder reaction?

L2 = 0.40                        # was 0.30
yh = -(0.30 + L2) * 0.8          # keep the hand at 80% of full reach
Show solution

Weak: peak $R_s=31.7,\ 32.6,\ 33.3\ \mathrm N$ as $L_2$ goes $0.20\to0.30\to0.40\ \mathrm m$. Here the reaction is governed by the limb's total weight and the dynamics of the swing, not by how the length is divided between the segments — a reminder to test which parameters actually move a result before tuning them.

K5 — static versus moving. Probes: the dynamic amplification a static snapshot misses — the inertial terms of §3 (§4).

From a single run, compare the shoulder reaction at release (where the limb is momentarily at rest) with its peak during the swing.

from lab import run                     # the section 7.4 script as a function

h = run()
WL = (2.0 + 1.5)*9.81
rs0, pk = h["Rs"][0], h["Rs"].max()
print(f"at release (at rest): {rs0:.2f} N = {rs0/WL:.2f} W_L")
print(f"peak mid-swing:       {pk:.2f} N = {pk/WL:.2f} W_L")
print(f"dynamic amplification: {pk/rs0:.2f}")
# -> at release (at rest): 11.64 N = 0.34 W_L
# -> peak mid-swing:       32.61 N = 0.95 W_L
# -> dynamic amplification: 2.80
Show solution

At release, where the limb is at rest, $R_s=11.6\ \mathrm N=0.34\,W_L$ — the static value. Early in the inward sweep ($t=0.16\ \mathrm s$, hand at $x_2=0.346\ \mathrm m$) the inertial terms push it to $32.6\ \mathrm N=0.95\,W_L$, a factor of $2.8$. A static calculation systematically under-reads what a moving joint carries; this is exactly why §4 noted that walking and running raise peak hip loads to $3$–$5\,W$.

K6 — swing harder. Probes: how speed (through release amplitude) feeds the centripetal term and the reaction (§3.3).

Release the limb from progressively larger initial angles and record the peak shoulder reaction.

from lab import run             # run() builds its own release pose

WL = (2.0 + 1.5)*9.81
for amp in (10, 20, 30, 40, 50):           # degrees off the hanging pose
    pk = run(amp=amp)["Rs"].max()
    print(f"amp={amp:3d} deg   peak Rs = {pk:6.2f} N = {pk/WL:.2f} W_L")
# -> amp= 10 deg   peak Rs =  20.66 N = 0.60 W_L
# -> amp= 20 deg   peak Rs =  22.37 N = 0.65 W_L
# -> amp= 30 deg   peak Rs =  25.75 N = 0.75 W_L
# -> amp= 40 deg   peak Rs =  32.61 N = 0.95 W_L
# -> amp= 50 deg   peak Rs =  48.39 N = 1.41 W_L
Show solution

The peak reaction climbs with amplitude: $0.60,\ 0.65,\ 0.75,\ 0.95,\ 1.41\,W_L$ for release angles $10^\circ$–$50^\circ$. A bigger swing reaches a higher speed at the bottom, so the centripetal demand — the $\dot J_c\dot q$ term of §3.3 — and with it the joint reaction grow faster than linearly.

K7 — how fast does it swing. Probes: that a constrained limb is an effective pendulum, but not the naive point-mass one (§1).

Measure the period of the constrained swing (twice the time to the first turning point) and compare it with a simple pendulum whose length is the limb's centre-of-mass distance. Take care over what counts as the turning point, because the hand does not start by moving inward. Bone 1, bone 2 and the rail form an offset slider-crank, and the $40^\circ$ release pose sits just short of the slider's outermost reach, so $x_2$ first rises — from $0.3584$ to $0.3600\ \mathrm m$ — and turns over about $3.7^\circ$ into the swing, at $t=0.073\ \mathrm s$. That is real kinematics and not solver drift: the constraint error never exceeds $10^{-6}\ \mathrm m$ (problem K9), and the same maximum appears with the Baumgarte gains set to zero. It does mean the first sign change of $\dot x_2$ is that outward maximum, and doubling it gives $0.15\ \mathrm s$. The turning point is the first minimum of $x_2$.

import numpy as np
from lab import run

h = run()
v = np.diff(h["x2"])                       # hand velocity along the rail
# The turning point is the first MINIMUM of x2, i.e. the first time the
# hand velocity flips negative -> positive.  The hand moves OUTWARD first
# (the linkage is an offset slider-crank released just short of full
# reach), so testing for any sign change instead catches that maximum at
# t = 0.07 s and gives 0.15 s.
i = np.flatnonzero((v[:-1] < 0) & (v[1:] >= 0))[0] + 1
L1, L2, m1, m2, g = 0.30, 0.30, 2.0, 1.5, 9.81
L_com = (m1*L1 + m2*(L1 + L2))/(m1 + m2)
print(f"first turning point at t = {h['t'][i]:.3f} s")
print(f"T_limb   = {2*h['t'][i]:.2f} s")
print(f"L_com    = {L_com:.2f} m")
print(f"T_simple = {2*np.pi*np.sqrt(L_com/g):.2f} s")
# -> first turning point at t = 0.756 s
# -> T_limb   = 1.51 s
# -> L_com    = 0.43 m
# -> T_simple = 1.31 s
Show solution

The hand reaches its innermost point at $t=0.756\ \mathrm s$, so the constrained limb's period is $2\times0.756=1.51\ \mathrm s$; a simple pendulum of length $L_{\text{com}}=0.43\ \mathrm m$ gives $\approx1.31\ \mathrm s$. The limb is the slower of the two: its mass is spread out and the constraint geometry adds effective inertia, so a point mass at the centre of mass underestimates the period. The single remaining degree of freedom still behaves like a pendulum — just not the naive one.

K8 — make the floor one-sided. Probes: the difference between a bilateral constraint and a real (unilateral) contact — the $\lambda_3\ge0$ condition (§7.7, §8).

A real floor can only push. After each solve, check the sign of the contact multiplier $\lambda_3$. From what release amplitude does it go negative — meaning the bilateral rail is 'pulling' the hand down, so a one-sided floor would let it lift off?

from lab import run

for amp in (30, 40, 50):                   # release angle (deg)
    lo = run(amp=amp)["Nc"].min()          # lam_3 over the whole swing
    note = "  <- lift-off" if lo < 0 else ""
    print(f"amp={amp} deg   min lambda_3 = {lo:6.2f} N{note}")
# -> amp=30 deg   min lambda_3 =  10.71 N
# -> amp=40 deg   min lambda_3 =   6.21 N
# -> amp=50 deg   min lambda_3 =  -5.88 N  <- lift-off
Show solution

At small swings the contact stays positive (minimum $10.7\ \mathrm N$ at $30^\circ$, $6.2\ \mathrm N$ at $40^\circ$). At $50^\circ$ it dips to $-5.9\ \mathrm N$: the two-sided rail is now pulling the hand down to hold it on the line — something a real floor cannot do, so the hand separates. Enforcing the inequality $\lambda_3\ge0$ (releasing the constraint when it would go negative) is the unilateral-contact upgrade of §7.7 and §8.

K9 — why the stabilization term. Probes: why the acceleration-level constraint needs Baumgarte feedback in floating point (§7.3).

Turn off the Baumgarte stabilization ($\gamma_d=\gamma_p=0$) and watch the constraint error $\max|g|$ over time; compare it with the stabilized run.

from lab import run

on = run()                                 # gd = gp = 40 (the default)
off = run(gd=0.0, gp=0.0)                  # Baumgarte disabled
print(f"stabilized   max|g| = {on['gerr'].max():.2e} m"
      f"   (final {on['gerr'][-1]:.2e})")
print(f"unstabilized max|g| = {off['gerr'].max():.2e} m"
      f"   (final {off['gerr'][-1]:.2e})")
print(f"factor = {off['gerr'].max()/on['gerr'].max():.0f}x")
# -> stabilized   max|g| = 1.03e-06 m   (final 6.51e-07)
# -> unstabilized max|g| = 2.16e-05 m   (final 2.16e-05)
# -> factor = 21x
Show solution

The acceleration-level constraint only pins $\ddot g=0$, so in floating point any small error in $g$ or $\dot g$ is never corrected and accumulates. With stabilization the drift stays at $\approx1\ \mu\mathrm m$ ($1.03\times10^{-6}\ \mathrm m$) for the whole swing and is still falling at the end of the run; without it the error reaches $2.2\times10^{-5}\ \mathrm m$, a factor of $21$ larger, and unlike the stabilized error it never comes back: it is at its maximum on the last step, and grows over longer runs. The correction $-2\gamma_d\,(J_c\dot q)-\gamma_p^2 g$ acts like a spring-damper on the constraint residual, with $\gamma_p$ setting its stiffness and $\gamma_d$ its damping; $\gamma_d=\gamma_p$ is the critically damped choice.

K10 — add a third bone. Probes: that the method scales unchanged — only the matrix grows — toward a full musculoskeletal model (§8).

Add a third bone (a hand-held tool of length $L_3=0.25\ \mathrm m$ carrying $m_3=1.0\ \mathrm{kg}$ at its tip, the Appendix values) with its own length constraint, and drop the rail to $y_h=-0.68\ \mathrm m$ so the tip can reach it. Release from the same $40^\circ$ pose with bone 2 hanging vertically. How large does the KKT system become, what does a single solve return, and does the proximal-carries-more ranking of §7.5 survive the extra link?

import numpy as np

L1, L2, L3 = 0.30, 0.30, 0.25              # bone lengths (m)
m1, m2, m3 = 2.0, 1.5, 1.0                 # point masses (kg)
g, yh, dt, nstep = 9.81, -0.68, 5e-5, 40000
M = np.diag([m1, m1, m2, m2, m3, m3])      # 6 x 6, still constant
Q = np.array([0, -m1*g, 0, -m2*g, 0, -m3*g], float)


def cons(q):                               # 4 rows now, not 3
    x1, y1, x2, y2, x3, y3 = q
    return np.array([0.5*(x1*x1 + y1*y1 - L1*L1),
                     0.5*((x2-x1)**2 + (y2-y1)**2 - L2*L2),
                     0.5*((x3-x2)**2 + (y3-y2)**2 - L3*L3),
                     y3 - yh])


def Jc(q):                                 # 4 x 6
    x1, y1, x2, y2, x3, y3 = q
    return np.array([[x1, y1, 0, 0, 0, 0],
                     [-(x2-x1), -(y2-y1), x2-x1, y2-y1, 0, 0],
                     [0, 0, -(x3-x2), -(y3-y2), x3-x2, y3-y2],
                     [0, 0, 0, 0, 0, 1.]], float)


def dJc(q, dq):
    a1, b1, a2, b2, a3, b3 = dq
    return np.array([[a1, b1, 0, 0, 0, 0],
                     [-(a2-a1), -(b2-b1), a2-a1, b2-b1, 0, 0],
                     [0, 0, -(a3-a2), -(b3-b2), a3-a2, b3-b2],
                     [0, 0, 0, 0, 0, 0.]], float)


th = np.radians(-90.0 + 40.0)              # same 40 deg release
x1, y1 = L1*np.cos(th), L1*np.sin(th)
x2, y2 = x1, y1 - L2                       # bone 2 hangs vertically
x3 = x2 + np.sqrt(L3*L3 - (yh - y2)**2)
q, dq = np.array([x1, y1, x2, y2, x3, yh]), np.zeros(6)
hist = {"Rs": [], "Re": [], "Rw": [], "Nc": []}
for step in range(nstep):
    J, dJ, gv = Jc(q), dJc(q, dq), cons(q)
    A = np.block([[M, J.T], [J, np.zeros((4, 4))]])         # 10x10 KKT
    rhs = np.concatenate([Q, -(dJ@dq) - 80.0*(J@dq) - 1600.0*gv])
    sol = np.linalg.solve(A, rhs)
    ddq, lam = sol[:6], -sol[6:]
    for key, val in zip(hist, (abs(lam[0])*L1, abs(lam[1])*L2,
                               abs(lam[2])*L3, lam[3])):
        hist[key].append(val)
    dq, q = dq + dt*ddq, q + dt*(dq + dt*ddq)

h = {k: np.array(v) for k, v in hist.items()}
seat = np.flatnonzero(h["Nc"] < 0)         # lam_4 < 0: the tip would lift off
end = seat[0] if seat.size else nstep
print("KKT is 10 x 10: 6 accelerations and 4 multipliers per solve")
print("release: " + "  ".join(f"{k} {h[k][0]:6.2f}" for k in h))
print(f"seated until t = {end*dt:.2f} s")
print("peaks:   " + "  ".join(f"{k} {h[k][:end].max():6.2f}" for k in h))
# -> KKT is 10 x 10: 6 accelerations and 4 multipliers per solve
# -> release: Rs  19.06  Re   5.26  Rw   2.90  Nc  11.55
# -> seated until t = 1.81 s
# -> peaks:   Rs  66.49  Re  41.46  Rw  16.68  Nc  19.87
Show solution

Six coordinates and four constraints make the KKT matrix $10\times10$, and one solve returns all the forces at once: at release, shoulder $19.1\ \mathrm N$, elbow $5.3\ \mathrm N$, wrist $2.9\ \mathrm N$, contact $11.6\ \mathrm N$. The bilateral rail multiplier $\lambda_4$ turns negative at $t=1.81\ \mathrm s$, so the tip would leave a real one-sided floor there (problem K8 again); over the seated window the peaks are $66.5$, $41.5$, $16.7$ and $19.9\ \mathrm N$. The proximal-carries-more ranking of §7.5 not only survives, it sharpens: each joint carries the weight and the inertia of everything distal to it, so the ordering shoulder $\gt$ elbow $\gt$ wrist is forced by the model, not observed in it. Note also that the peak shoulder reaction has doubled ($32.6\to66.5\ \mathrm N$) for a limb only 29 % heavier: the extra link swings on a longer arm, and its inertial contribution grows faster than its mass. Nothing about the method changed from §7; only the sizes of $M$, $J_c$ and the system. The same fifty lines scale from this toy to a research-grade model, and what changes is the realism of those matrices, the subject of §8.

Parameters and constants used throughout the module are collected in the Appendix.

Appendix — notation and parameters

A single reference for the whole module: the symbols in one place, then every numerical value used in the worked examples and the computational lab, then the threads that tie this module to its neighbours.

A. Notation

Symbols are defined at first use in the text; this table gathers them. Sizes refer to a system with $n$ generalized coordinates and $m$ constraints.

SymbolMeaningIntroduced
$q,\ \dot q,\ \ddot q$generalized coordinates, velocity, acceleration§1
$g(q)=0$holonomic constraint(s); $g_1,g_2,\dots$ individually§1
DOF $=n-m$degrees of freedom = coordinates − independent constraints§1
$f$joint mobility; a synovial joint removes $6-f$ freedoms§2
$M(q)$mass / inertia matrix (symmetric, positive-definite)§3
$c(q,\dot q)$Coriolis, centrifugal and gravity terms (the bias)§3
$Q$generalized applied force (muscles, external loads)§3
$J_c=\partial g/\partial q$constraint Jacobian ($m\times n$)§3
$\lambda$Lagrange multipliers — the constraint-force intensities§3
$J_c^{\mathsf T}\lambda$generalized constraint (joint reaction) force§3
$F_J$ (JRF), $R_s$, $R_e$joint reaction force; shoulder, elbow reactions $=|\lambda_i|L_i$§4, §7.2
$W$body weight; $W_L=(m_1+m_2)g$ the limb's own weight§4, §7.5
$p,\ A_c,\ E^*,\ \nu$contact pressure, contact area, effective modulus, Poisson's ratio§5
$\beta,\ S=\tan\beta$socket rim angle; stability ratio§6
$F_{ab},\ a,\ b,\ \alpha$abductor force; its moment arm; the center-of-mass offset; its line-of-action tilt from vertical§4.2
$R_{\text{eff}},\ p_0,\ a$effective contact radius; Hertz peak pressure; Hertz contact radius§5.2
$N,\ F_t,\ \varphi,\ \theta_n$socket compressive load; destabilizing sideways force; resultant tilt from the socket axis; bony-neck half-angle§6.1
$\gamma_d,\ \gamma_p$Baumgarte constraint-stabilization gains (damping, restoring)§7.3

Symbol reuse, resolved: $g$ is the gravitational acceleration everywhere except in $g(q)$, the constraint function, which always carries its argument. $W$ is body weight and $W_L$ the limb's own weight. Two collisions that existed in draft have been removed rather than flagged: the Baumgarte gains are $\gamma_d,\gamma_p$, not $\alpha,\beta$, so $\alpha$ is only the abductor line-of-action tilt of §4.2 and $\beta$ only the socket rim angle of §6. The one remaining reuse is $a$: the abductor moment arm in §4.2 and the Hertz contact radius in §5.2. They never appear in the same equation, and the Hertz radius always carries its formula (5.2) beside it.

C. Where this connects

  • Builds on Module 1 (forces, torques, free-body diagrams, the muscle moment-arm disadvantage) and Module 2 (the beam stresses a bone carries once the joint reaction is known).
  • Feeds Module 4 (cartilage as a biphasic, lubricated contact — taking the joint reaction of §4 as its input), Module 6 (ligaments and tendons as compliant springs), and Module 8 (gait inverse dynamics, with measured segment inertias). The full map of which idealization each later module repays is in §8.
